title: Learning Arbitrary Lindbladians from Time Evolution
abstract: We study the problem of learning an unknown Markovian open-system generator from access to its physical time evolution. This generator, called a Lindbladian, contains Hamiltonian and dissipative coefficients indexed by an exponentially large family of possible Pauli terms. We propose an efficient algorithm that learns arbitrary Lindbladians from time evolution under minimal assumptions. For a Lindbladian of dynamical strength at most $Λ$, the algorithm estimates every coefficient to error $ε$ using $\widetilde O(Λ^2/ε^2)$ experiments and $\widetilde O(Λ/ε^2)$ total evolution time, together with polynomial classical running time. The algorithm consists of two nonadaptive, ancilla-free, and control-free stages: 1. The support-learning stage outputs a candidate support of size $\mathrm{poly}(Λ/η)$ that contains every Hamiltonian and dissipative coordinate of magnitude at least $η$, using $\widetilde O(Λ^2/η^2)$ experiments with preparations of product Pauli eigenstates and single-qubit Pauli measurements. 2.The coefficient-learning stage estimates all coefficients in any candidate support of size $M$ to error $ε$, using $\widetilde O(Λ^2\log M/ε^{2})$ experiments with preparations of random stabilizer states and measurements in random Clifford bases. Composing the two stages identifies and estimates every coefficient of an arbitrary Lindbladian in polynomial time. The experiment-count and total-evolution-time scalings match the lower bounds up to logarithmic factors, so the algorithm is nearly optimal for learning arbitrary Lindbladians.
summary: This paper presents an efficient algorithm to reconstruct the full Lindbladian generator of an open quantum system solely by measuring its time evolution. By breaking the problem into identifying relevant coefficients (support learning) and then estimating their values, the authors achieve resource scalings that match theoretical lower bounds for arbitrary dynamics.
main_problem: The core problem is learning an unknown Markovian open-system generator (Lindbladian) entirely from access to its physical time evolution measurements.
main_result: The authors propose an efficient, nearly optimal algorithm that can estimate every coefficient of an arbitrary Lindbladian in polynomial time relative to the dynamical strength bound ($\Lambda$) and required accuracy ($\epsilon$).
method: The algorithm is structured in two stages: first, a support-learning stage identifies candidate coefficients above a threshold $\eta$, followed by a coefficient-learning stage estimates these candidates using random stabilizer states.
model_or_system: The system involves open quantum systems whose dynamics are governed by a Lindbladian master equation. The coefficients include Hamiltonian terms $\{h_a\}$ and dissipative terms $\{\gamma_{ab}\}$, indexed by Pauli operators.
key_observables: Lindbladian coefficients ($\{h_a\}, \{\gamma_{ab}\}$), time evolution $e^{t\mathcal{L}}$, and measurement outcomes from product Pauli eigenstates or random stabilizer states.
important_parameters: Dynamical strength bound $\Lambda$, desired accuracy $\epsilon$, and the support recovery threshold $\eta$.
main_assumptions: The only prior information is an upper bound $\Lambda$ on the dynamical strength of the Lindbladian. The method assumes access to nonadaptive, ancilla-free, control-free time evolution measurements.
figures_summary: Not specified in the provided notes; the results are summarized by resource scaling comparisons (Table 1) showing polynomial dependence on $\Lambda/\epsilon$.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem of Lindbladian learning and presents a two-stage algorithm: Theorem 1.1 details the support-learning stage, followed by Theorem 1.2 for coefficient estimation, culminating in a corollary that combines both stages for arbitrary Lindbladians.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful theoretical tool to characterize complex quantum dynamics (open systems) when direct Hamiltonian measurement is impossible, which is crucial for interpreting experimental results from trapped ions or superconducting qubits.
